cards.title: Heap Data Structure
cards.teaser: A heap is a complete binary tree where every node satisfies the heap property relative to its children. It is stored compactly in an array and supports insert and extract in O(log n) — making it the foundation of priority queues and sorting algorithms.

runs.text: A
heap
is a binary tree with two invariants: (1) it is
complete
— every level is fully filled except possibly the last, which fills left-to-right — and (2) every node satisfies the
heap property
with respect to its children. The completeness invariant is what makes array storage practical: there are no gaps, so the tree maps perfectly to contiguous indices.

Because the root always holds the extreme value (minimum in a min-heap, maximum in a max-heap), retrieval of that value is O(1). Insert and extract both disturb the invariant temporarily and restore it in O(log n) steps — proportional to the tree's height, which is always ⌊log₂ n⌋ for a complete binary tree.

explanation.code:
import heapq

# Python's heapq gives a min-heap on a plain list
nums = [5, 1, 8, 3, 2]
heapq.heapify(nums)        # O(n) in-place
print(nums)                # [1, 2, 8, 3, 5]  — heap-ordered, not sorted
print(nums[0])             # 1 — minimum always at index 0

runs.text: Heaps are
not
sorted arrays. The heap property only guarantees that each node is smaller (or larger) than its children — siblings have no ordering guarantee. The array
is a valid min-heap even though 8 appears before 3 and 5.

A heap is the most efficient data structure when you need repeated access to the minimum (or maximum) of a changing collection. If you need the full sorted order, sort instead. If you only need the extremum repeatedly, use a heap.

A heap is a binary tree where the smallest (or largest) value always floats to the top. It is stored as an array — no pointers needed — and guarantees O(log n) insert and O(log n) removal of the top element. Think of it as a constantly-maintained tournament bracket where the winner is always at position zero.

cards.title: Min-Heap vs Max-Heap
cards.teaser: A min-heap keeps the smallest element at the root; a max-heap keeps the largest. All other nodes satisfy the same local rule relative to their subtree. The two variants are mirrors of each other — choose based on whether you need fast access to the minimum or the maximum.

runs.text: In a
min-heap
, every node's value is less than or equal to the values of its children. The root holds the global minimum. In a
max-heap
, every node's value is greater than or equal to its children's values; the root holds the global maximum.

explanation.code:
# Min-heap example (Python's default)
min_heap = [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]
# Tree view:
#        1
#      /   \
#     3     5
#    / \
#   7   9
# Every parent ≤ its children → valid min-heap

# Max-heap example (same values)
max_heap = [9, 7, 5, 3, 1]
# Tree view:
#        9
#      /   \
#     7     5
#    / \
#   3   1
# Every parent ≥ its children → valid max-heap

runs.text: Both variants support the same operations in the same asymptotic time. The only difference is the comparison direction:

items.text: Min-heap
— use for shortest-path algorithms (Dijkstra), event schedulers, and finding the k smallest elements.
Max-heap
— use for finding the k largest elements, implementing a max-priority queue, or heapsort in ascending order.

runs.text: Python's heapq only implements a min-heap. To get max-heap behavior, negate all values on the way in and negate again on the way out. This is covered in card 11.

Min-heap and max-heap are the same structure with the comparison flipped. In a min-heap the smallest value sits at the top; in a max-heap the largest does. Pick the one that matches what you need to extract quickly.

cards.title: Heap Property
cards.teaser: The heap property is the local ordering constraint that every node must satisfy with respect to its immediate children — not the whole tree. In a min-heap: parent ≤ both children. In a max-heap: parent ≥ both children. Maintaining this invariant through inserts and deletes is the core work of a heap.

runs.text: The
heap property
is a local invariant: for every node
i

with children, the node's value must compare favorably to each child. In a min-heap, "favorably" means "less than or equal to." The property does not say anything about sibling relationships or cousins — only parent-to-child.

explanation.code:
def is_min_heap(arr: list[int]) -> bool:
    """Check whether arr satisfies the min-heap property."""
    n = len(arr)
    for i in range(n // 2):          # only internal nodes have children
        left  = 2 * i + 1
        right = 2 * i + 2
        if left < n and arr[i] > arr[left]:
            return False              # parent > left child: violation
        if right < n and arr[i] > arr[right]:
            return False              # parent > right child: violation
    return True

print(is_min_heap([1, 2, 8, 3, 5]))   # True
print(is_min_heap([1, 5, 2, 8, 3]))   # True
print(is_min_heap([3, 2, 8, 1, 5]))   # False (3 > 2's child 1)

runs.text: The heap property implies the global minimum is always at the root, because every ancestor of any node is smaller. However, no path constraint exists between siblings:
arr[left]
and
arr[right]
can appear in any order.

The heap property's locality is what makes sift-up and sift-down efficient. After an insert or extract, only one path from root to leaf (or leaf to root) is out of order. Fixing it takes O(log n) comparisons, not O(n).

The heap property is a simple parent-wins rule: in a min-heap, every parent must be smaller than or equal to both its children. That single local rule, applied everywhere, guarantees the global minimum is always at the root. Siblings can be in any order — only the parent-child relationship is constrained.

cards.title: Heap as an Array
cards.teaser: A heap is stored as a plain array without pointers. For a node at index i (1-based): parent is at i//2, left child at 2i, right child at 2i+1. In 0-based indexing: parent at (i-1)//2, children at 2i+1 and 2i+2. This layout makes heap operations cache-friendly and avoids memory allocation.

runs.text: Because a heap is a
complete

binary tree, every level above the last is full and the last level fills left-to-right. This means there are no gaps — the tree maps to a contiguous array with a simple arithmetic formula for navigation.

explanation.code:
# 0-based indexing (Python's heapq convention)
# For node at index i:
#   parent:      (i - 1) // 2
#   left child:   2*i + 1
#   right child:  2*i + 2

heap = [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 10, 11]

#          1        ← index 0
#        /   \
#       3     5     ← indices 1, 2
#      / \   / \
#     7   9 10  11  ← indices 3, 4, 5, 6

i = 1  # node with value 3
print("parent:", heap[(i - 1) // 2])   # heap[0] = 1
print("left:",   heap[2 * i + 1])      # heap[3] = 7
print("right:",  heap[2 * i + 2])      # heap[4] = 9

runs.text: The array representation has several practical advantages:

items.text: No pointer overhead
— each node uses one array slot, not three (value + left pointer + right pointer).
Cache locality
— parent and both children sit within a small array region, so sift operations have good cache behavior.
Simple resize
— appending a new element to the end of the array corresponds exactly to adding a new leaf at the next available position in the complete tree.

runs.text: Textbooks often use 1-based indexing (parent at i//2, children at 2i and 2i+1) because the formulas are cleaner. Python's heapq uses 0-based indexing. Either works — just stay consistent within an implementation.

You don't need nodes and pointers for a heap — a plain list is enough. Because the tree is always complete, the parent of any element at index i lives at (i-1)//2, and its children live at 2i+1 and 2i+2. Simple arithmetic replaces pointer traversal entirely.

cards.title: Heapify — O(n) Bottom-Up Construction
cards.teaser: Building a heap from an unsorted array takes O(n) time using bottom-up heapify, not O(n log n). Start from the last internal node and sift each node down. The key insight: most nodes are near the bottom of the tree and travel very short distances.

runs.text: The naive approach to building a heap is to start with an empty heap and insert each element one by one. Each insert is O(log n), giving O(n log n) total.
Bottom-up heapify
does better by working in reverse: treat the array as an already-complete binary tree, then repair the heap property starting from the last internal node (index n//2 - 1) down to the root.

The O(n) proof is the key insight: about half the nodes are leaves and do zero work. A quarter are at height 1 and do O(1) work. An eighth are at height 2 and do O(2) work. Summing the geometric series
Σ (n/2^h) × h
converges to O(n), not O(n log n).
Python's heapq.heapify() uses this exact bottom-up algorithm and runs in O(n). If you have a list ready, always prefer heapify() over inserting elements one by one.

Building a heap from scratch is O(n), not O(n log n). The trick: start at the bottom of the tree and sift each node down into place. Most nodes are near the leaves and barely move, so the total work sums to linear. Python's heapq.heapify() does exactly this.

cards.title: Heap Insert — Sift-Up
cards.teaser: Inserting into a heap takes O(log n): append the new value at the end of the array (maintaining completeness), then sift it up by repeatedly swapping it with its parent while it is smaller (min-heap). The new element travels at most O(log n) levels.

runs.text: Inserting into a heap has two phases:
place
and
sift-up
. Appending to the end maintains the completeness invariant. Sifting up restores the heap property by bubbling the new value toward the root until it is no longer smaller than its parent.

explanation.code:
def heap_push(heap: list[int], val: int) -> None:
    heap.append(val)          # Step 1: place at the end
    _sift_up(heap, len(heap) - 1)

def _sift_up(heap: list[int], i: int) -> None:
    while i > 0:
        parent = (i - 1) // 2
        if heap[i] < heap[parent]:    # child is smaller: swap
            heap[i], heap[parent] = heap[parent], heap[i]
            i = parent
        else:
            break                     # heap property restored

heap = [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]
heap_push(heap, 2)
print(heap)  # [1, 3, 2, 7, 9, 5]  — 2 sifted up past 5

runs.text: In the worst case the new value is the global minimum and travels all the way to the root —
O(log n)

swaps. In the best case (new value is already larger than its parent) zero swaps occur — O(1). The expected number of swaps for a random insert into a random heap is O(1), making inserts very fast in practice.
heapq.heappush(heap, item) performs exactly this operation. It is the idiomatic way to insert into a Python min-heap.

To insert into a heap, append the new value at the end, then keep swapping it with its parent as long as it is smaller than the parent. The value bubbles up to its correct position. At most it travels the full height of the tree — O(log n) swaps.

cards.title: Extract-Min — Sift-Down
cards.teaser: Extracting the minimum from a min-heap takes O(log n): swap the root with the last element, shrink the heap by one, then sift the new root down by repeatedly swapping it with its smaller child until the heap property is restored.

runs.text: Popping the minimum has three phases: (1) record the root value (the minimum), (2) move the last element to the root position to maintain completeness, (3)
sift-down
the new root by swapping it with its smallest child until it no longer violates the heap property.
The sift-down always picks the
smaller
child to swap with. This is critical: swapping with the larger child would leave that larger child above the smaller one, violating the heap property in the other subtree.
heapq.heappop(heap) implements this in C, making it significantly faster than a pure-Python version. Always prefer the standard library for heap operations.

To remove the minimum, swap the root with the very last element, then shrink the array by one. The new root is probably out of place, so push it down by swapping it with whichever child is smaller — keep going until it lands in a spot where both children are at least as large. That path is at most O(log n) long.

cards.title: Python's heapq Module
cards.teaser: Python's heapq module implements a min-heap on top of a plain list. It provides heappush, heappop, heapify, nlargest, nsmallest, and heapreplace — all operating in-place on a list you supply. There is no separate heap class.

runs.text: The
heapq
module is in the Python standard library. It treats any list as a min-heap, provided you only modify it through
heapq
functions. The module does not enforce this — mutating the list directly will silently corrupt the heap invariant.

explanation.code:
import heapq

# --- Build ---
data = [5, 1, 8, 3, 2, 9, 4]
heapq.heapify(data)           # O(n) in-place; data is now heap-ordered

# --- Insert ---
heapq.heappush(data, 0)       # O(log n)
print(data[0])                 # 0 — new minimum

# --- Extract minimum ---
print(heapq.heappop(data))     # 0    O(log n)
print(heapq.heappop(data))     # 1

# --- Peek without removing ---
print(data[0])                 # the current minimum; O(1)

# --- Push then pop in one step (more efficient than two calls) ---
result = heapq.heapreplace(data, 6)   # pops min, pushes 6; O(log n)
print(result)                  # the old minimum

runs.text: Key behaviors to remember:

items.text: Min-heap only
— heapq has no max-heap mode. Negate values to simulate one.
In-place on a list
— heapq.heapify([]) returns None; it modifies the list in-place.
Peek is free
— data[0] reads the minimum in O(1) without disturbing the heap.
Tuples work
— heapq compares tuples lexicographically, so (priority, item) is the standard pattern for priority queues.

runs.text: heapq is implemented in C for CPython via _heapq, falling back to a pure-Python version when the C extension is unavailable. In practice, it is very fast.

Python's heapq module turns an ordinary list into a min-heap. You pass the list to heapq functions rather than calling methods on a heap object. heapify() sets it up, heappush() adds an element, heappop() removes the smallest. Always use these functions — never sort or append to the list directly.

cards.title: heapq.nlargest and nsmallest
cards.teaser: heapq.nlargest(n, iterable) and heapq.nsmallest(n, iterable) return the n largest or smallest elements from any iterable in O(k log n) time. They are more efficient than sorting when k is much smaller than the total size.

runs.text: Finding the top-k elements from a large collection is a recurring pattern in data processing.
heapq.nlargest(k, iterable)
and
heapq.nsmallest(k, iterable)
handle this efficiently using a size-k heap that keeps only the candidates seen so far.

explanation.code:
import heapq

scores = [42, 7, 95, 31, 88, 14, 73, 56, 100, 22]

print(heapq.nlargest(3, scores))    # [100, 95, 88]
print(heapq.nsmallest(3, scores))   # [7, 14, 22]

# Works on any iterable with a key function
words = ["banana", "fig", "apple", "cherry", "kiwi"]
print(heapq.nlargest(2, words, key=len))   # ['banana', 'cherry']

# Comparing strategies by size:
# k ≪ n  → nlargest/nsmallest: O(n log k)
# k ≈ n  → sorted():           O(n log n)  (faster in practice)
# k == 1 → max() / min():      O(n)        (always prefer these)

runs.text: Under the hood,
nsmallest(k, it)

maintains a max-heap of size k. For each element in the iterable it checks whether the element is smaller than the heap's maximum; if so, it replaces the max and sifts down. Total: O(n log k) comparisons.

If k is close to n, Python's heapq documentation itself recommends sorted(iterable)[:k] — the sort has a lower constant factor than repeated heap operations in that regime. For small k (single digits to a few hundred), nlargest and nsmallest clearly win.

heapq.nlargest(k, data) scans the whole list once but only keeps track of the k biggest values seen so far using a small heap. It is faster than sorting when k is small — O(n log k) instead of O(n log n). For k = 1, just use max() or min() — they are O(n) with no heap overhead.

cards.title: Priority Queue Use Cases
cards.teaser: A priority queue is an abstract data type where each element has a priority, and the next element dequeued is always the one with the highest (or lowest) priority. Heaps are the canonical implementation. Core applications: Dijkstra's shortest path, A* search, job scheduling, event simulation, and the top-K pattern.

runs.text: A
priority queue

differs from a regular queue (FIFO) in that dequeue returns the element with the best priority, regardless of insertion order. Heaps implement this in O(log n) per operation, making them practical for algorithms that repeatedly need the "best" next item.
Common priority queue use cases:

items.text: Dijkstra / A*
— always expand the lowest-cost (or lowest f-score) node next. A priority queue replaces a naive O(V²) search.
Job schedulers
— always run the highest-priority or shortest-job-first task. OS schedulers, Celery task queues, and Kubernetes pods all use this pattern.
Event-driven simulation
— events are stamped with a future time; the heap always surfaces the next event to process.
Top-K streaming
— maintain a size-k heap over an unbounded data stream to track the k largest elements seen so far in O(n log k).
Huffman coding
— repeatedly merge the two lowest-frequency trees; a min-heap gives the right pair each time.

runs.text: Python's standard library also ships queue.PriorityQueue, which wraps heapq in a thread-safe class. For single-threaded code, use heapq directly — it has lower overhead.

A priority queue is a queue where every item has a priority and the next item out is always the one with the best priority — not the one that waited longest. Heaps make this O(log n) per operation. Dijkstra's algorithm is the canonical example: always expand the closest unvisited node, which a min-heap surfaces instantly.

cards.title: Max-Heap with heapq — Negate Values
cards.teaser: Python's heapq only supports min-heaps. Simulate a max-heap by negating every value on the way in and negating again on the way out. The smallest negated value is the largest original value, so heappop() returns the maximum.

runs.text: Since
heapq
always pops the
smallest
value, negating all values before insertion makes the largest original value become the smallest negated value. Popping and negating the result gives the maximum.

explanation.code:
import heapq

# Max-heap via negation
max_heap: list[int] = []

def push_max(heap: list[int], val: int) -> None:
    heapq.heappush(heap, -val)   # negate on the way in

def pop_max(heap: list[int]) -> int:
    return -heapq.heappop(heap)  # negate on the way out

for v in [5, 1, 8, 3, 9, 2]:
    push_max(max_heap, v)

print(pop_max(max_heap))  # 9
print(pop_max(max_heap))  # 8
print(pop_max(max_heap))  # 5

# With tuples: negate only the priority key
tasks = [(3, 'low'), (1, 'urgent'), (2, 'normal')]
max_pq: list = []
for priority, name in tasks:
    heapq.heappush(max_pq, (-priority, name))

print(heapq.heappop(max_pq))  # (-3, 'low') → highest priority first

runs.text: The negation trick works for integers, floats, and any totally ordered type. For tuples, only negate the priority component, not the entire tuple. Be careful with strings: negation is not defined for them. Wrap string values in a comparison class or use a numeric priority key instead.

The negation trick is idiomatic Python but easy to get wrong. A common bug is forgetting to negate on pop, returning a negative value. Wrap push_max and pop_max in helper functions to encapsulate the negation and prevent caller errors.

Python's heap only gives you the smallest value, but you can fake a max-heap by flipping the sign of every number before inserting. The biggest number becomes the smallest when negated, so heappop() hands it back first. Negate it again and you have the original maximum.

cards.title: d-ary Heaps and Fibonacci Heaps
cards.teaser: A d-ary heap generalizes the binary heap to d children per node — a 4-ary heap halves the number of sift-down comparisons at the cost of more work per level. A Fibonacci heap achieves amortized O(1) insert and decrease-key, making Dijkstra's algorithm run in O(E + V log V) — the best known complexity for dense graphs.

runs.text: The binary heap is the most common heap in practice, but two important variants exist for specialized performance needs.
A
d-ary heap
allows each node to have up to
d
children instead of 2. The height of the tree shrinks to log_d(n), so sift-up (insert) becomes faster: O(log_d n) comparisons. However, sift-down (extract) must find the minimum among
d

children at each level, costing O(d log_d n). For workloads dominated by inserts (e.g., Dijkstra on sparse graphs), a 4-ary heap often outperforms a binary heap in practice due to better cache utilization — the four children of a node are fetched in the same cache line.

explanation.code:
# d-ary heap index arithmetic (0-based, d children per node)
# For node at index i with branching factor d:
#   parent:     (i - 1) // d
#   k-th child: d*i + k + 1   for k in range(d)

d = 4  # 4-ary heap

def parent(i: int) -> int:
    return (i - 1) // d

def children(i: int, n: int) -> list[int]:
    return [d * i + k + 1 for k in range(d) if d * i + k + 1 < n]

runs.text: A
Fibonacci heap
is a more complex structure that achieves amortized O(1) for insert and
decrease-key

operations, and O(log n) for extract-min. The key benefit is decrease-key in O(1) amortized, which allows Dijkstra's algorithm to run in O(E + V log V) — optimal for dense graphs. In practice, Fibonacci heaps have large constant factors and are rarely used outside of theoretical contexts or extremely performance-sensitive graph libraries.

items.text: Binary heap
— O(log n) insert, O(log n) extract-min, O(log n) decrease-key. Best for general use.
d-ary heap (d=4)
— lower height, better cache behavior for insert-heavy workloads.
Fibonacci heap
— O(1) amortized insert and decrease-key. Theoretically optimal for Dijkstra on dense graphs; rarely used in practice.

runs.text: For nearly all production code, Python's heapq (binary min-heap) is the right choice. Reach for d-ary heaps or Fibonacci heaps only when profiling proves a bottleneck in heap operations on very large graphs.

A d-ary heap gives each node d children instead of 2 — it is shorter and wider, so insert is faster but extract-min does more work per level. A Fibonacci heap is a theoretically beautiful structure where insert and decrease-key cost O(1) amortized, enabling faster Dijkstra on large graphs. Both are advanced variants; the standard binary heap in heapq is the right starting point for almost every real-world problem.
